extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical philosophy, literature, and translation; writers seeking archetypal models from Plato
extracted.subtask_description: Use Plato's Book VIII portraits of states and corresponding individuals as archetypal templates for character and polity depiction — including their origins, dominant passions, social dynamics, and symbolic devices (e.g., number/harmony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocracy (State) — outward resemblance to the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: “The new form of government resembles the ideal in obedience to rulers and contempt for trade, and having common meals, and in devotion to warlike and gymnastic exercises.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key signals of a timocratic polity: formal obedience to rulers, disdain for commerce, communal meals, and emphasis on martial/gymnastic training. Also note corruption of philosophy and the replacement of arts of peace by arts of war. Use these concrete institutions and priorities to render a believable timocratic State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocratic man — traits and origin story
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is self-asserting and ill-educated, yet fond of literature, although not himself a speaker,—fierce with slaves, but obedient to rulers, a lover of power and honour... fond, too, of gymnastics and of hunting. As he advances in years he grows avaricious, for he has lost philosophy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To portray a timocratic individual, combine martial virtues (courage, love of honour) with poor education and rising avarice; show domestic origins (father retired from politics, mother urging ambition, servant inculcating manliness) to explain his temperament and ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy (State) — origin and structural evils
rubrics_metrics.description: “The rule is of the rich only... the decline begins with the possession of gold and silver; illegal modes of expenditure are invented... riches outweigh virtue... two nations are struggling together in one—the rich and the poor... the greatest evil... a man may sell his property and have no place in the State.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict oligarchy by foregrounding wealth as the organising principle: legal exclusion, concentration of privilege, widespread poverty, social division (paupers and rogues), and governance failures stemming from bad education and bad laws. Use economic practices and law to show decline of civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchic man — moral economy and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is mean, saving, toiling, the slave of one passion ... If he is the trustee of an orphan, and has the power to defraud, he will soon prove that he is not without the will... Hence he leads a divided existence; in which the better desires mostly prevail. But when he is contending for prizes... he is afraid to incur a loss.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize oligarchic individuals through stinginess, obsession with wealth, moral ambivalence (better desires present but subordinated), and risk-aversion in public life. Show how lack of education and slavish desires produce social exploitation (drones, rogues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy (State) — manner of life and political character
rubrics_metrics.description: “The manner of life in such a State is that of democrats; there is freedom and plainness of speech, and every man does what is right in his own eyes... The State is not one but many, like a bazaar... The great charm is, that you may do as you like.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render democratic settings via variety, informal manners, egalitarian speech, and a marketplace-like multiplicity of lifestyles. Emphasize lack of training for statesmen, equality among unequals, and the triumph of individual preference over shared civic standards as characteristic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic man — pleasures, instability, and susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “He divides his time impartially between [necessary and unnecessary pleasures]... sometimes he takes to drink, and then he turns abstainer; he practises in the gymnasium or he does nothing at all... ‘Every thing by starts and nothing long.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray democratic individuals as impulsive, variety-seeking, and fickle — oscillating between extremes of behaviour. Use the distinction between necessary and unnecessary pleasures to show moral ambivalence and the absence of steady principles, and illustrate vulnerability to demagogy and mob influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny (State) and the tyrant — origin from democracy and nature of rule
rubrics_metrics.description: “Tyranny springs from democracy... the protector... makes his well-known request to them for a body-guard... having crushed all his rivals, stands proudly erect in the chariot of State, a full-blown tyrant... He is enabled to depress the poor by heavy taxes... Then comes unpopularity... he has to make a purgation of the State... he will take the slaves from their owners and make them his body-guard.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To depict tyranny, show the transition from popular protector to concentrated power: use scenes of demagogy, manufactured crises, granting of extraordinary guard/force, purges of rivals, appropriation of temple/family wealth, tax burdening of poor, and recruitment of loyal but socially marginal guards. Emphasize the structural and moral degradations that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrant (individual) — psychology of power and misery
rubrics_metrics.description: “The tyrant... is the negation of government and law... his life as an obscene dream... the more hated he is, the more he will require trusty guards... he is a parricide and a cruel, unnatural son... this ideal of wickedness living in helpless misery.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a tyrant, balance external power with inner helplessness: paranoia, dependence on paid or enslaved guards, cruel acts (even against family), and a miserable, suspicious existence despite dominion. Use rhetorical exaggeration and tragic irony to heighten the contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical gradation and mapping between States and souls
rubrics_metrics.description: “Each of these governments and individuals has a corresponding ethical gradation: the ideal State is under the rule of reason... in the timocracy... the constitution... is based, first, upon courage, and secondly, upon the love of honour... in the second stage... the love of gain has succeeded to them; in the third... the various passions are allowed to have free play; at last... tyranny.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mapping device (state ↔ individual ↔ passion) to structure character arcs and political allegory: associate dominant passions (reason, courage, avarice, appetite, single monstrous passion) with corresponding institutional forms to dramatize moral decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel technique and metaphorical language (style device)
rubrics_metrics.description: “He describes in a succession of parallels between the individuals and the States... The eighth book of the Republic abounds in pictures of life and fanciful allusions; the use of metaphorical language is carried to a greater extent than anywhere else in Plato.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt parallelism between individual psychology and political forms as a compositional strategy; employ vivid metaphors, family portraits, and emblematic details (drones, beasts, bazaars, temple-fable) to compress complex social dynamics into memorable images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platonic number and musical/arithmetical symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the so-called number of the State: a ‘human or imperfect number’ with four terms and three intervals, references to 3, 4, 5, the Pythagorean triangle, cubes yielding 216, and harmonies producing numbers like 400 and 8000; music as a symbol of the harmony of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerical and musical symbolism (ratios, harmonies, Pythagorean motifs, tetractys) as a symbolic framework for structuring generational, civic, or mythic cycles. If employing the Device, reproduce specific numeric motifs (3–4–5 triangle, 216, 8000) or analogous symbolic architectures to signal order/decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character origin via upbringing and social influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated emphasis on origins: influence of parents (retired statesman father, ambitious mother), household servants, education (good or bad), and social disorders as causes of individual types and state constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing believable archetypes, embed formative scenes: parental exhortations, social humiliations, educational environments, and gossip or counsel from servants/peers. These micro-histories should plausibly explain dominant passions and later public behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid portrait touches and rhetorical surprises
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted as Plato’s happiest touches: e.g., the drones of two kinds, the tyrant as parricide, the animals in democracy acting as equals, the rhetorically surprising comparisons and family vignettes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete, surprising details and idiosyncratic images (humiliating domestic scenes, animal metaphors, unexpected cruelty or comic inversion) to make typological portraits memorable and affective. These 'touches' function as heuristics for authentic-sounding classical portraits.
